headline: Appledore's ledges still holding cod while the flats give up stripers after dark
subhead: Thirteen miles of coast, one boat, and the shoals are still paying off if you're willing to run before sunrise.
body_markdown:
People from away look at a map of this state's coastline and figure there's nothing here worth trailering a boat for. Thirteen miles, they say, like it's a punchline. I've fished from the Merrimack line to the Piscataqua for going on twenty years now and I can tell you those thirteen miles stretch about as far as you let them. The Isles of Shoals alone are six miles offshore and hold more structure than most fleets see in a season — ledges, humps, boulder fields, current lines that split around Appledore and White Island like something's down there deciding where the fish go. I run my 20-foot Lund out of Rye Harbor most mornings before the sun's up, and I fish it like the run to the Shoals is nothing, because out here it isn't.

This week the pattern held about like I expected — I said last time it'd hold 72 hours and it's basically still doing that, groundfish steady, stripers pushed into a nighttime program same as everywhere south of us, just a little later to the party because our water hasn't gone through the mid-70s the way the Sound and the Jersey beaches have. That's the whole story of the Gulf of Maine in July — everybody else is dealing with warm, stratified water pushing bass deep and nocturnal, and we're sitting here in the low-to-mid 60s still getting some daytime action, just softer than June.

Cod fishing off the Shoals has been the most dependable thing I've touched all week. I've been working the ledges south and east of Appledore, 60 to 90 feet, right on the slack before the tide turns — that's the window, twenty minutes either side of dead slack, because once that current starts ripping around those boulders you can't hold bottom with anything less than a pound of lead and you spend more time re-rigging than fishing. Jigging diamond jigs, the 6- to 8-ounce depending on drift speed, tipped with a chunk of clam or mackerel belly if I've got it. Cod have been running 3 to 8 pounds, with a couple of better ones — one push past 10 on Tuesday morning that about pulled the rod out of my hands over the rail. Haddock mixed in on the same drifts, smaller average size right now, mostly a pound and a half to three pounds, but steady enough that a few boats have been limiting out before 9 a.m. Whiting show up on the same bottom and I don't mind them — good eating, and they keep the rod bent between the better bites.

Mackerel have been thick around the Shoals moorings and along the edges of White Island — small ones, schoolies really, but there's enough bait there that it's worth jigging up a dozen before you set the drift for cod. Fresh mackerel belly outfishes anything from the bait shop on those ledges, no question.

Stripers are the trickier read right now. Daytime bites along Great Boars Head and the beach south of Hampton have gone soft the last week and a half — not dead, just inconsistent, a fish here and there on umbrella rigs and bunker chunks fished off the bottom on the outgoing. The better program has shifted to first light and last light, which tracks with what's happening everywhere from here to Jersey — warm surface water, fish sliding onto structure and feeding in low light instead of grinding it out at noon. I've had my best luck working the mouth of Hampton Harbor on the last two hours of the incoming tide, right around dusk, throwing swimming plugs and soft plastic paddletails on 3/4-ounce jigheads along the edge of the channel where it meets the flats. Fish have been 24 to 32 inches mostly, with a few slot fish mixed in, holding tight to the deeper cut where the tide funnels bait past the jetty rocks.

The Piscataqua has actually been a bright spot for stripers willing to work current. Below the Memorial Bridge and down past the Coast Guard station, the tide rips hard enough to hold fish on structure all day, not just dawn and dusk — the moving water and depth keep it cooler and more oxygenated than the open beaches, so the bite's held up better through the heat. Bucktails, half-ounce to an ounce depending on the stage of tide, bounced along the bottom near the pilings and rock piles, have been picking up stripers to 30 inches on both the ebb and flood, best window being the last two hours of ebb when bait gets flushed down through the narrows.

Odiorne Point has been quiet for bass but decent for flounder — small boat guys anchoring up over the mud-sand mix off the point, squid strips and clam on a simple two-hook bottom rig, picking away at winter flounder and a few blackback in that 12- to 14-inch range. Nothing to write home about, but a nice change of pace and good eating.

No bluefish to speak of in close yet, which surprises me given what's happening south of us — the blitz tearing up bunker from Jersey through the Sound hasn't pushed this far north in any real numbers, though I'd keep an eye on the outer beaches over the next couple weeks if bunker schools keep working up the coast the way they have been.

Looking ahead, I don't see much reason for this pattern to break. Water's stable, no big blow in the forecast, tides are building back toward the next moon. If you want groundfish, get to the Shoals ledges on the slack — that window's short and it's the whole game. If you want stripers, fish the Piscataqua current or work the Hampton Harbor mouth on that evening incoming. I'll be doing both, probably before most of you finish your coffee.
